visible.name: Jonas Eberhart
visible.line: Jonas Eberhart, 27, is the founder of a three-person consumer hardware studio in a quiet workshop, making a design-led portable induction burner meant to replace gas flames in small apartments.

project.title: Ember
project.logline: A slim, quiet portable induction burner with a machined knob and a glass top, designed for small kitchens; a hundred early owners have one, with 700 people on the mailing list.
constraints: The seed round of 600,000 dollars covers about twenty months at the current burn.
Custom tooling for the glass top costs 52,000 dollars and takes twelve weeks at the factory.
Electrical certification must be planned from the start, and the test lab takes ten weeks.
The team is three people: Jonas, an industrial designer and a part-time operations lead.
The first run is capped at 300 units because the factory books capacity by season.

tone_requests.text: Take your time; I would rather have a considered answer than a fast one.
Write in full sentences, no bullet lists.
Tell me how it reads or feels before telling me what to change.
Don't rush me to a decision; lay out what is at stake first.
Be honest about taste: tell me when something is merely fine.
Quote my own words back when two things I said conflict.

stated_views.text: A product should feel finished the day it ships.
Most hardware startups fail from sloppiness, not from slowness.
The box is part of the product, and so is the manual.
Data tells you what happened, not what is good.
Owners remember how it felt, not what it cost.

new_work.text: Here's my draft investor update, titled "A note from the workshop." It tells the story of choosing a matte finish for our portable induction burner and has one photo and no numbers. Is leaving out the numbers a mistake?

I've finished twelve long interviews about our induction burner. Most owners praise the knob feel, two found the glass surface scratched in a month, and one said it looked "like furniture." How should I synthesize this for the team?

I'm writing the pitch narrative for a meeting on Friday. The company makes a design-led portable induction burner for small apartments. Should it open with the object on the table or with the story of why a burner needs to look this good?
I need a job post for our first industrial designer. We're a team of three in a quiet studio and I want it to read like how we work. I have a page. Is it too long?
Our launch plan is a single film and ten press contacts in the autumn, no discount, full price. The mailing list has 700 people. Is that enough to be heard?

I'm designing the pricing page. The unit costs 190 dollars to build well, and I plan to hold it at 349 dollars. I want a short story about what the price buys. Should it go above or below the buy button?
The factory says tooling for the glass top will take twelve weeks and cost 52,000 dollars. A catalog glass top lets me ship in six. What would you do?
A customer emailed that the knob feels slightly loose after a month. I'd like to reply tomorrow with a considered letter and send a replacement. Is a day too long to wait?
I'm choosing packaging for the first 300 units. A rigid box with a custom foam-free insert costs 9 dollars a unit; a plain one costs 2. I think the box is the first product. Is 9 too much?
We need a warranty policy for the page. I'd like two years and free repairs instead of refunds. What are the risks to cash?
I have to choose which two of five details to finish for the first run: a brushed knurled knob, a flush power switch, an etched logo, a cable that tucks away, a matte glass finish. Which two?
I'm writing the waitlist email announcing the ship date slips six weeks for a finish problem. I'd like it to be honest and warm. Here's a draft with three paragraphs. Is it too long?
A design magazine asked for a unit and an interview. I'd like to send an object in a box with a handwritten note. Should I wait until the finish is perfect?
A retailer wants 200 units on consignment at 45 percent. I have only sold direct. The shop is lovely but the display is cluttered. Should I take it?
I'm drafting a private letter to the first fifty owners asking what they'd change. I do not want a survey. How should I phrase the first sentence?
The manual draft is a 32-page booklet with illustrations. A friend says nobody reads it. Is a booklet an indulgence, or part of the product?
Our first batch had a small color variation on the knob. Do I scrap them, offer them at a discount, or tell owners the finish varies?
I'm writing a thank-you note to our first hundred owners. I'd like it handwritten for each, and it takes a day for ten. Is that a good use of time?
My cofounder wants to run paid ads to hit our sales target. I'd rather build word of mouth through owners. How should we settle this?
I have a ninety-second film script: hands, a pan, the glass top, a quiet boil. No narration. I'd like it to feel still and considered. What would you change?
A design school wants to feature the burner in a class and asks for ten units at cost. It would make the work known but costs about 1,900 dollars. Do I do it?
I'm choosing between a considered photography day with a studio for 2,400 dollars and a small trade show booth. Which one?
Here's a slide with a product photo and six lines of text about materials. I'd like to cut it to the photo and one line. Does the slide still work?
I need to tell the factory their last batch had a visible seam on the glass. I'd like to be direct but warm; we visit them each quarter. Here's a draft. How do I fix the tone?
I'm writing my answer to "why will you win?" for an accelerator form. Limit 100 words. My draft leans on the quality of the object. Is that enough?
Planning the next season: one big bet, finishing the glass, with a quiet stretch to complete it. Is it a mistake to say no to everything else for twelve weeks?
